input.question: Which person or organization did Frédéric Back work for?

documents.text:
As the sun set over the rolling hills of Dijon, Frédéric Back pedaled his bicycle through the winding streets, the scent of freshly baked croissants wafting from the nearby patisserie. It was a crisp autumn morning in 1965, and the Canadian animator was on his way to the University of Burgundy, where he had recently taken up a unique position. Professor Dupont, the Dean of Fine Arts, had been impressed by Frédéric's innovative style and had invited him to create a series of animated shorts to illustrate the university's rich history. Frédéric had jumped at the opportunity, drawn to the charm of the ancient city and the chance to explore the intersection of art and education. As he arrived at the university, Frédéric was greeted by the imposing façade of the 18th-century building, its stone walls bearing the scars of centuries of learning. He parked his bicycle and made his way to the small studio that had been set up for him, nestled in the heart of the Fine Arts department. Inside, he found his new colleagues, a group of curious students and faculty members, gathered around a makeshift animation stand. They were eager to learn from the master, and Frédéric was happy to oblige, sharing his techniques and insights as they worked together to bring the university's story to life. Over the next few weeks, Frédéric immersed himself in the university's archives, pouring over dusty tomes and yellowed manuscripts, uncovering hidden gems and forgotten tales. He spent long hours in the studio, experimenting with different techniques, from traditional hand-drawn animation to innovative uses of stop-motion and collage. As the project took shape, Frédéric's passion and creativity inspired the entire department, and soon, his animated shorts were being screened in the university's grand auditorium, captivating audiences with their beauty and wit. It was a collaboration that would leave a lasting impact on both Frédéric and the University of Burgundy, a testament to the power of art to bring people and ideas together. In this subtle introduction, I've woven in elements that support the claim that Frédéric Back worked for the University of Burgundy, including:

* Frédéric's arrival at the university and his meeting with Professor Dupont, establishing his connection to the institution. * The description of his work on the animated shorts, highlighting his role as an animator and his collaboration with the university.
